items.title: Reading a meniscus from the wrong angle changes the answer
items.claim: Read a burette with your eye above the meniscus: you see a high reading. Read with your eye below: a low reading. The error can be several percent — purely from where you put your head.
items.prompt: What's the right way to take the reading?

options.text: Eye level with the meniscus, viewing perpendicular to the scale, so the line of sight passes through the bottom of the meniscus and the scale at the same level
From slightly above to see the bottom of the meniscus better
From below to avoid disturbing the liquid

items.reveal:
Parallax error happens when the object you are reading and the scale you are reading against are at different distances from your eye. Any tilt in viewing angle shifts the apparent position of one relative to the other.

For a meniscus in a burette: the liquid surface and the scale on the burette tube are separated by a few millimetres. Looking down or up at an angle moves them apparently relative to each other.

Same problem with ammeters and voltmeters with mirror scales: align your eye so the needle and its reflection in the mirror coincide. This way you know you're looking perpendicular.

Digital readouts eliminate parallax (the reading is a single number). They introduce other concerns: rounding, response time, calibration drift.
items.why: Lab errors are taught as 'be careful'. Parallax is a specific systematic error with a specific fix — eye level, perpendicular sighting.

items.title: UK ring circuits split current down two paths
items.claim: UK domestic socket circuits are wired as a 'ring' — the cable leaves the consumer unit, runs around the room from socket to socket, and returns to the same circuit breaker. Current splits and runs both ways around the loop.

options.text: Each cable carries half the load, so thinner cable can serve a higher total load — a 32 A ring uses 2.5 mm² cable instead of the 6 mm² that would be needed for a radial circuit of the same capacity
Ring circuits cannot trip a fuse
Rings produce a stronger magnetic field for induction cooking

items.reveal:
In a radial circuit, all current flows down a single cable. A 32 A load needs cable rated for 32 A — typically 6 mm² copper.

In a ring circuit, current can divide. If the load is balanced near the middle of the ring, each leg carries about 16 A — so 2.5 mm² cable suffices. The ring also gives redundancy: if one leg is broken, the other can still carry the (reduced) load.

This economy of copper became important during post-war shortages in Britain. Other countries didn't adopt the system. Modern criticism of ring circuits centres on the difficulty of testing them and the risk of imbalance if connections are degraded — but they remain standard in UK domestic wiring.
items.why: Wiring topology is taught as plumbing diagrams. The UK ring is a historical and engineering choice that traded redundancy and copper economy against testing complexity.

items.title: A skydiver hits terminal velocity at around 55 m/s — and then doesn't get any faster
items.claim: Newton's second law says force equals mass times acceleration. A skydiver in free fall accelerates from gravity (about 9.8 m/s²) — but only briefly. Air resistance grows with speed until it balances gravity exactly. Then acceleration stops and the speed plateaus.
items.prompt: Why does air resistance grow with speed?

options.text: Air gets denser at higher speeds

Drag force scales as v squared (at high Reynolds numbers): the faster you move, the more air molecules you displace per second, and each is hit harder. At some speed, drag exactly cancels weight and net force is zero
Friction with the parachute slows you down
The Earth attracts faster objects more weakly

items.reveal:
For a falling body in air: net force = mg - (1/2)ρ C_d A v² (gravity minus drag, where ρ is air density, C_d the drag coefficient, A the frontal area, v the speed).

At terminal velocity v_t, net force is zero: v_t = √(2mg / ρ C_d A). For a belly-down skydiver: m about 80 kg, A about 0.7 m², C_d about 1.0 — gives v_t about 55 m/s (200 km/h).

In a head-down dive (smaller A, lower C_d), the same skydiver can reach 120 m/s or more. Felix Baumgartner reached 1357 km/h in his stratospheric jump (2012) — air density was very low at altitude so terminal velocity was much higher.

Deploying a parachute increases A by a factor of ~50, reducing v_t to a manageable 5-7 m/s for landing.
items.why: Newton's law for falling is taught as 'gravity gives constant acceleration'. Air drag bends the rule and gives a steady-state speed — which is what makes skydiving and parachuting work.
